title: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair
source: Inflammation LS5009  lectures 1 and 2 student copy.pdf

cards.explanation: They coordinate signalling between immune and other host cells; they are not all made exclusively by leukocytes.
cards.text: Soluble protein mediators regulating the activity of other cells are {{c1::cytokines}}.
cards.question: Soluble protein mediators regulating the activity of other cells are {{c1::cytokines}}.

cards.explanation: Chemokines are cytokines, while not every cytokine is a chemokine.
cards.text: The cytokine subfamily directing cell migration is the {{c1::chemokines}}.
cards.question: The cytokine subfamily directing cell migration is the {{c1::chemokines}}.

cards.explanation: Chemokines guide leukocytes towards sites of infection or tissue injury.
cards.text: Directed movement along a chemical concentration gradient is {{c1::chemotaxis}}.
cards.question: Directed movement along a chemical concentration gradient is {{c1::chemotaxis}}.

cards.explanation: The source includes recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes as examples.
cards.text: Inflammatory chemokines can recruit leukocytes from blood into {{c1::damaged or infected tissues}}.
cards.question: Inflammatory chemokines can recruit leukocytes from blood into {{c1::damaged or infected tissues}}.

cards.explanation: The pathway is drawn through STAT4 and T-bet. These are contextual teaching pathways, not exclusive rules for every in-vivo setting.
cards.text: In the simplified differentiation diagram, IL-12 favours {{c1::Th1}} development.
cards.question: In the simplified differentiation diagram, IL-12 favours {{c1::Th1}} development.

cards.explanation: It links the depicted IL-12 signal with a Th1 cytokine programme.
cards.text: The Th1 transcription factor labelled in the diagram is {{c1::T-bet}}.
cards.question: The Th1 transcription factor labelled in the diagram is {{c1::T-bet}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram places IL-4/STAT6 upstream; the source is a schematic, not a complete differentiation protocol.
cards.text: The transcription factor linked with Th2 differentiation is {{c1::GATA3}}.
cards.question: The transcription factor linked with Th2 differentiation is {{c1::GATA3}}.

cards.explanation: The simplified source places IL-6/TGF-β and STAT3 upstream.
cards.text: The transcription factor linked with Th17 development is {{c1::RORγt}}.
cards.question: The transcription factor linked with Th17 development is {{c1::RORγt}}.

cards.explanation: The source links this programme with IL-2/TGF-β and STAT5.
cards.text: The transcription factor marking the illustrated induced regulatory T-cell programme is {{c1::Foxp3}}.
cards.question: The transcription factor marking the illustrated induced regulatory T-cell programme is {{c1::Foxp3}}.

cards.explanation: The diagram associates this with IL-6/STAT3 and Tfh differentiation.
cards.text: The factor labelled in the T follicular helper pathway is {{c1::Bcl6}}.
cards.question: The factor labelled in the T follicular helper pathway is {{c1::Bcl6}}.

cards.explanation: The source links Tfh help with antibody production.
cards.text: The Tfh cytokine supporting the illustrated B-cell response is {{c1::IL-21}}.
cards.question: The Tfh cytokine supporting the illustrated B-cell response is {{c1::IL-21}}.

cards.explanation: The figure also shows mucus production and effects on eosinophils, basophils and epithelia.
cards.text: Th2-associated IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 support responses including {{c1::worm expulsion}}.
cards.question: Th2-associated IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 support responses including {{c1::worm expulsion}}.

cards.explanation: The source uses a broad effector schematic; not every listed response is a direct action on every cell.
cards.text: The characteristic Th1 cytokine activating macrophage-associated defences is {{c1::IFN-γ}}.
cards.question: The characteristic Th1 cytokine activating macrophage-associated defences is {{c1::IFN-γ}}.

cards.explanation: It acts through tissue-cell chemokine responses supporting defence against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
cards.text: Th17-derived IL-17 helps promote {{c1::neutrophil recruitment}}.
cards.question: Th17-derived IL-17 helps promote {{c1::neutrophil recruitment}}.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with simply treating all cytokines as uniformly pro-inflammatory.
cards.text: The illustrated iTreg response uses IL-10 and TGF-β to {{c1::suppress T-cell responses}}.
cards.question: The illustrated iTreg response uses IL-10 and TGF-β to {{c1::suppress T-cell responses}}.

cards.explanation: It involves host cells, blood vessels and plasma/tissue proteins.
cards.text: Inflammation is a protective response of {{c1::vascularised living tissue}} to injury or infection.
cards.question: Inflammation is a protective response of {{c1::vascularised living tissue}} to injury or infection.

cards.explanation: Necrosis, trauma, foreign material and immune reactions are among the lecture’s triggers; inflammation and infection are not synonyms.
cards.text: Inflammation can occur without infection, for example after {{c1::sterile tissue injury}}.
cards.question: Inflammation can occur without infection, for example after {{c1::sterile tissue injury}}.

cards.explanation: Adaptive responses can interact with it; the distinction is not that chronic inflammation excludes innate cells.
cards.text: The rapid inflammatory response is a major component of {{c1::innate immunity}}.
cards.question: The rapid inflammatory response is a major component of {{c1::innate immunity}}.

cards.explanation: The response also depends on the host, rather than the agent alone.
cards.text: Stimulus dose, potency and exposure duration influence the {{c1::inflammatory response}}.
cards.question: Stimulus dose, potency and exposure duration influence the {{c1::inflammatory response}}.

cards.explanation: The slide gives malnutrition and Chediak–Higashi syndrome as examples. It is not a complete account of the syndrome’s cell biology.
cards.text: Poor nutrition and defective leukocyte function can impair {{c1::host defence}}.
cards.question: Poor nutrition and defective leukocyte function can impair {{c1::host defence}}.

cards.explanation: Its goals include toxin inactivation and restoration of function, not merely producing redness.
cards.text: Alongside containing injury and eliminating microbes, inflammation prepares tissue for {{c1::repair}}.
cards.question: Alongside containing injury and eliminating microbes, inflammation prepares tissue for {{c1::repair}}.

cards.explanation: The same protective mechanisms may contribute to disease if excessive, misplaced or persistent.
cards.text: Uncontrolled inflammatory responses can cause {{c1::host tissue damage}}.
cards.question: Uncontrolled inflammatory responses can cause {{c1::host tissue damage}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture distinguishes these from recruited circulating cells.
cards.text: Resident connective-tissue sentinels include macrophages and {{c1::mast cells}}.
cards.question: Resident connective-tissue sentinels include macrophages and {{c1::mast cells}}.

cards.explanation: Fibronectin, laminin and proteoglycans are other named matrix components.
cards.text: The extracellular matrix contains structural proteins such as collagen and {{c1::elastin}}.
cards.question: The extracellular matrix contains structural proteins such as collagen and {{c1::elastin}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to another item in the source: platelets participate in inflammation but are cell fragments, not white blood cells.
cards.text: Fibrinogen and C-reactive protein are examples of inflammatory {{c1::plasma proteins}}.
cards.question: Fibrinogen and C-reactive protein are examples of inflammatory {{c1::plasma proteins}}.

cards.explanation: The mediator table links NO with vasodilation and, in host defence, microbial killing.
cards.text: Nitric oxide can relax vascular {{c1::smooth muscle}}.
cards.question: Nitric oxide can relax vascular {{c1::smooth muscle}}.

cards.explanation: This is one reason inflammatory activation requires regulation.
cards.text: Reactive oxygen species can kill microbes but also injure {{c1::host tissue}}.
cards.question: Reactive oxygen species can kill microbes but also injure {{c1::host tissue}}.

cards.explanation: Recruitment brings phagocytes to the site, whereas phagocytosis is an effector function performed once targets are encountered.
cards.text: Engulfment of microbes or debris by a cell is {{c1::phagocytosis}}.
cards.question: Engulfment of microbes or debris by a cell is {{c1::phagocytosis}}.

cards.explanation: This is a characteristic pattern, not a universal rule for every pathogen or hypersensitivity reaction.
cards.text: The predominant early leukocytes in typical acute inflammation are {{c1::neutrophils}}.
cards.question: The predominant early leukocytes in typical acute inflammation are {{c1::neutrophils}}.

cards.explanation: This accompanies leukocyte emigration and often produces oedema.
cards.text: Acute inflammation typically involves exudation of fluid and {{c1::plasma proteins}}.
cards.question: Acute inflammation typically involves exudation of fluid and {{c1::plasma proteins}}.

cards.explanation: Chronic inflammation also combines injury with vascular/fibroblast proliferation and attempted repair.
cards.text: Macrophages and lymphocytes predominate in the typical {{c1::chronic inflammatory infiltrate}}.
cards.question: Macrophages and lymphocytes predominate in the typical {{c1::chronic inflammatory infiltrate}}.

cards.explanation: Increased local blood flow contributes to its appearance.
cards.text: The cardinal sign rubor means {{c1::redness}}.
cards.question: The cardinal sign rubor means {{c1::redness}}.

cards.explanation: Vasodilation and greater blood flow help explain it; local warmth is distinct from systemic fever.
cards.text: Calor describes local {{c1::heat}}.
cards.question: Calor describes local {{c1::heat}}.

cards.explanation: Here the term refers to oedema and cellular accumulation, not necessarily a neoplasm.
cards.text: Tumor in the classical inflammatory signs means {{c1::swelling}}.
cards.question: Tumor in the classical inflammatory signs means {{c1::swelling}}.

cards.explanation: Tissue distortion, pressure and chemical mediators can all contribute.
cards.text: Dolor is the inflammatory sign of {{c1::pain}}.
cards.question: Dolor is the inflammatory sign of {{c1::pain}}.

cards.explanation: Pain, swelling and tissue injury may limit movement or other local functions.
cards.text: The fifth cardinal sign is {{c1::loss of function}}.
cards.question: The fifth cardinal sign is {{c1::loss of function}}.

cards.explanation: Microbial infection is not required; damaged or dying cells can initiate sterile inflammation.
cards.text: Ischaemic tissue necrosis can trigger {{c1::acute inflammation}}.
cards.question: Ischaemic tissue necrosis can trigger {{c1::acute inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: It promotes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.
cards.text: The vasoactive amine released prominently from mast cells is {{c1::histamine}}.
cards.question: The vasoactive amine released prominently from mast cells is {{c1::histamine}}.

cards.explanation: By contrast, GM-CSF and G-CSF in the same source list are colony-stimulating cytokines, not chemokines.
cards.text: IL-8, also called CXCL8, is a {{c1::chemokine}}.
cards.question: IL-8, also called CXCL8, is a {{c1::chemokine}}.

cards.explanation: Their effects also include leukocyte activation and systemic acute-phase responses.
cards.text: TNF and IL-1 promote leukocyte recruitment by activating the {{c1::endothelium}}.
cards.question: TNF and IL-1 promote leukocyte recruitment by activating the {{c1::endothelium}}.

cards.explanation: Prostaglandins can sensitise pain pathways; mechanical pressure is another contributor.
cards.text: The pain mediators emphasised are prostaglandins and {{c1::bradykinin}}.
cards.question: The pain mediators emphasised are prostaglandins and {{c1::bradykinin}}.

cards.explanation: The slide groups C3a and C5a under chemotaxis. C3a is chiefly an anaphylatoxin; it should not be treated as an equivalent major neutrophil chemoattractant.
cards.text: The complement fragment strongly associated with neutrophil chemotaxis is {{c1::C5a}}.
cards.question: The complement fragment strongly associated with neutrophil chemotaxis is {{c1::C5a}}.

cards.explanation: More blood flow produces local erythema and warmth.
cards.text: Increased arteriolar diameter during inflammation is {{c1::vasodilation}}.
cards.question: Increased arteriolar diameter during inflammation is {{c1::vasodilation}}.

cards.explanation: The resulting protein-rich fluid differs from a pressure-driven protein-poor transudate.
cards.text: Increased permeability permits plasma proteins to escape into the {{c1::extravascular tissue}}.
cards.question: Increased permeability permits plasma proteins to escape into the {{c1::extravascular tissue}}.

cards.explanation: Vasodilation initially increases flow; do not infer that vasodilation alone immediately means stasis.
cards.text: Fluid loss from vessels can concentrate red cells and contribute to slowed flow called {{c1::stasis}}.
cards.question: Fluid loss from vessels can concentrate red cells and contribute to slowed flow called {{c1::stasis}}.

cards.explanation: They concentrate antimicrobial substances and help trap microbes.
cards.text: The extracellular fibrillar networks released by neutrophils are {{c1::neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)}}.
cards.question: The extracellular fibrillar networks released by neutrophils are {{c1::neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs)}}.

cards.explanation: This differs from enclosing a microbe inside a phagocyte.
cards.text: NETs help limit microbial spread by {{c1::extracellular trapping}}.
cards.question: NETs help limit microbial spread by {{c1::extracellular trapping}}.

cards.explanation: The source contrasts increased hydrostatic pressure or reduced plasma oncotic pressure with inflammatory barrier leakage.
cards.text: Protein-poor fluid associated with altered pressure balance is a {{c1::transudate}}.
cards.question: Protein-poor fluid associated with altered pressure balance is a {{c1::transudate}}.

cards.explanation: It reflects altered vascular permeability and may contain inflammatory cells.
cards.text: Protein-rich inflammatory fluid is an {{c1::exudate}}.
cards.question: Protein-rich inflammatory fluid is an {{c1::exudate}}.

cards.explanation: Protein-rich inflammatory exudation instead implies a permeability change.
cards.text: Raised hydrostatic pressure or reduced plasma oncotic pressure favours {{c1::transudation}}.
cards.question: Raised hydrostatic pressure or reduced plasma oncotic pressure favours {{c1::transudation}}.

cards.explanation: Intercellular gaps open; the illustrated mediator-driven response is rapid and short-lived.
cards.text: Histamine can rapidly increase permeability through endothelial {{c1::contraction or retraction}}.
cards.question: Histamine can rapidly increase permeability through endothelial {{c1::contraction or retraction}}.

cards.explanation: This may cause more sustained leakage than the short mediator-driven gap response.
cards.text: Burns and some microbial toxins can increase leakage through direct {{c1::endothelial injury}}.
cards.question: Burns and some microbial toxins can increase leakage through direct {{c1::endothelial injury}}.

cards.explanation: It precedes rolling, firm adhesion and emigration.
cards.text: Movement of leukocytes towards the vessel wall during slowed flow is {{c1::margination}}.
cards.question: Movement of leukocytes towards the vessel wall during slowed flow is {{c1::margination}}.

cards.explanation: Selectin-mediated interactions allow repeated attachment and release.
cards.text: Transient weak endothelial interactions produce leukocyte {{c1::rolling}}.
cards.question: Transient weak endothelial interactions produce leukocyte {{c1::rolling}}.

cards.explanation: Their ligands are distinct from the firm-adhesion system.
cards.text: The adhesion molecules principally mediating rolling are {{c1::selectins}}.
cards.question: The adhesion molecules principally mediating rolling are {{c1::selectins}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to the slide: integrins bind endothelial ligands such as ICAM/VCAM, not selectins as their principal firm-adhesion partners.
cards.text: Activated leukocyte integrins primarily support {{c1::firm adhesion}}.
cards.question: Activated leukocyte integrins primarily support {{c1::firm adhesion}}.

cards.explanation: This is also called diapedesis and follows recruitment to the vessel wall.
cards.text: Crossing the endothelial barrier into tissue is {{c1::transmigration}}.
cards.question: Crossing the endothelial barrier into tissue is {{c1::transmigration}}.

cards.explanation: Chemotaxis directs movement within tissue; it is not identical to rolling along the endothelium.
cards.text: After leaving the vessel, recruited cells follow chemoattractant gradients towards the {{c1::injury or infection focus}}.
cards.question: After leaving the vessel, recruited cells follow chemoattractant gradients towards the {{c1::injury or infection focus}}.

cards.explanation: This is a recognised mechanism relevant to the prompt. The numbered image has no answer key, so the deck does not guess a one-to-one mapping of all seven labels.
cards.text: Activated leukocytes can increase permeability by damaging {{c1::endothelial cells}}.
cards.question: Activated leukocytes can increase permeability by damaging {{c1::endothelial cells}}.

cards.explanation: This is one of the standard permeability mechanisms asked for by the activity; it is distinct from passage through a gap between cells. The low-detail numbered image is not used as a precise label key.
cards.text: Increased vesicular transport through endothelial cells is {{c1::transcytosis}}.
cards.question: Increased vesicular transport through endothelial cells is {{c1::transcytosis}}.

cards.explanation: This links repair-associated angiogenesis with permeability. The activity supplies no complete labelled solution, so exact arrow assignments are not inferred.
cards.text: Newly formed vessels may leak while their endothelial junctions are {{c1::immature}}.
cards.question: Newly formed vessels may leak while their endothelial junctions are {{c1::immature}}.

cards.explanation: Pus includes dead/dying neutrophils, tissue debris, fluid and often microbes; it is not simply dead neutrophils alone.
cards.text: A localised collection of pus within tissue is an {{c1::abscess}}.
cards.question: A localised collection of pus within tissue is an {{c1::abscess}}.

cards.explanation: Their accumulation, antimicrobial activity and death contribute to the purulent material.
cards.text: The dominant recruited cells contributing to pus in a typical bacterial abscess are {{c1::neutrophils}}.
cards.question: The dominant recruited cells contributing to pus in a typical bacterial abscess are {{c1::neutrophils}}.

cards.explanation: Encapsulation and the local environment may limit immune access and antimicrobial penetration; the source’s claim that no antibiotics can enter is too absolute.
cards.text: An abscess wall can limit spread but also hinder {{c1::effective clearance}}.
cards.question: An abscess wall can limit spread but also hinder {{c1::effective clearance}}.

cards.explanation: The wall reflects inflammatory organisation and repair, not simply healthy neighbouring cells forming an impenetrable seal.
cards.text: A mature abscess can develop a surrounding {{c1::fibrous wall}}.
cards.question: A mature abscess can develop a surrounding {{c1::fibrous wall}}.

cards.explanation: Granulation tissue is a repair tissue, not a granuloma.
cards.text: New vessels, fibroblasts and loose matrix in a healing wound form {{c1::granulation tissue}}.
cards.question: New vessels, fibroblasts and loose matrix in a healing wound form {{c1::granulation tissue}}.

cards.explanation: The source’s days are approximate examples; healing phases overlap and vary with wound context.
cards.text: In the later illustrated wound stage, abundant {{c1::macrophages}} replace many early neutrophils.
cards.question: In the later illustrated wound stage, abundant {{c1::macrophages}} replace many early neutrophils.

cards.explanation: Migrating and proliferating endothelial cells support vascularisation of repair tissue.
cards.text: New blood-vessel formation during healing is {{c1::angiogenesis}}.
cards.question: New blood-vessel formation during healing is {{c1::angiogenesis}}.

cards.explanation: The source shows fibroblast migration/proliferation and later collagen deposition.
cards.text: The cells depositing much of the repair extracellular matrix are {{c1::fibroblasts}}.
cards.question: The cells depositing much of the repair extracellular matrix are {{c1::fibroblasts}}.

cards.explanation: Their contractile activity helps reduce the wound area.
cards.text: Wound contraction is associated with fibroblasts differentiating into {{c1::myofibroblasts}}.
cards.question: Wound contraction is associated with fibroblasts differentiating into {{c1::myofibroblasts}}.

cards.explanation: This covers the wound surface, unlike collagen scar production in the deeper connective tissue.
cards.text: Re-epithelialisation requires keratinocyte proliferation and {{c1::migration from wound margins}}.
cards.question: Re-epithelialisation requires keratinocyte proliferation and {{c1::migration from wound margins}}.

cards.explanation: Macrophages and local tissue cells supply additional signals as healing proceeds.
cards.text: Injured vessels and degranulating platelets provide growth factors that initiate {{c1::repair}}.
cards.question: Injured vessels and degranulating platelets provide growth factors that initiate {{c1::repair}}.

cards.explanation: Vascular endothelial growth factor supports endothelial responses and new-vessel formation.
cards.text: The growth factor especially linked with wound angiogenesis is {{c1::VEGF}}.
cards.question: The growth factor especially linked with wound angiogenesis is {{c1::VEGF}}.

cards.explanation: The source names EGF, TGF-α and HB-EGF; TGF-α should not be confused with TGF-β.
cards.text: EGF-family signals help promote wound {{c1::re-epithelialisation}}.
cards.question: EGF-family signals help promote wound {{c1::re-epithelialisation}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture includes knockout-mouse evidence for selected FGF/FGFR pathways. Those model results are not a complete clinical wound-healing treatment algorithm.
cards.text: FGF-family signals contribute to healing responses of epithelial and {{c1::connective-tissue cells}}.
cards.question: FGF-family signals contribute to healing responses of epithelial and {{c1::connective-tissue cells}}.

cards.explanation: The table presents platelet-derived growth factor as a repair-associated mitogen.
cards.text: The growth factor PDGF supports proliferation of fibroblasts and vascular {{c1::smooth-muscle cells}}.
cards.question: The growth factor PDGF supports proliferation of fibroblasts and vascular {{c1::smooth-muscle cells}}.

cards.explanation: Its biological actions depend on cell type and context; the table’s antiproliferative row does not mean it universally prevents scarring.
cards.text: A growth factor associated with inhibition of many cells in vitro but also strong fibrogenic effects is {{c1::TGF-β}}.
cards.question: A growth factor associated with inhibition of many cells in vitro but also strong fibrogenic effects is {{c1::TGF-β}}.

cards.explanation: This differs from the neutrophil-rich pus of a suppurative abscess.
cards.text: A thin fluid collection separating skin layers in the blister example illustrates {{c1::serous inflammation}}.
cards.question: A thin fluid collection separating skin layers in the blister example illustrates {{c1::serous inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: This describes the source example rather than the location of every possible blister.
cards.text: In the illustrated skin blister, serous fluid separates the epidermis from the {{c1::dermis}}.
cards.question: In the illustrated skin blister, serous fluid separates the epidermis from the {{c1::dermis}}.

cards.explanation: The source does not imply all exercise is harmful; the exposure/recovery context matters.
cards.text: Repeated severe exercise injury without adequate recovery may sustain {{c1::inflammation}}.
cards.question: Repeated severe exercise injury without adequate recovery may sustain {{c1::inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: The acute sequence instead illustrates transient infiltration/collagen and regenerated muscle. This is a model comparison, not a diagnosis from exercise alone.
cards.text: The chronic-injury muscle panels show accumulated collagen and {{c1::fibrosis}} rather than complete regeneration.
cards.question: The chronic-injury muscle panels show accumulated collagen and {{c1::fibrosis}} rather than complete regeneration.

cards.explanation: Pain occurs in some forms but is not required in every case.
cards.text: Immune-mediated inflammatory myopathies can cause muscle {{c1::weakness}}.
cards.question: Immune-mediated inflammatory myopathies can cause muscle {{c1::weakness}}.

cards.explanation: The slide contrasts this with neutrophils accumulating within alveoli.
cards.text: Congested lung vessels packed with erythrocytes illustrate the {{c1::vascular component}} of acute inflammation.
cards.question: Congested lung vessels packed with erythrocytes illustrate the {{c1::vascular component}} of acute inflammation.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with relatively empty air spaces in the normal reference.
cards.text: Neutrophils filling alveolar spaces illustrate the {{c1::cellular component}} of acute lung inflammation.
cards.question: Neutrophils filling alveolar spaces illustrate the {{c1::cellular component}} of acute lung inflammation.

cards.explanation: Infection or inhaled irritants can contribute; bronchitis is not automatically proof of a bacterial cause.
cards.text: Inflammation of the bronchi is {{c1::bronchitis}}.
cards.question: Inflammation of the bronchi is {{c1::bronchitis}}.

cards.explanation: The source compares the obstructed/inflamed airway with a clear normal airway.
cards.text: Mucus, inflammatory cells and debris in inflamed airways contribute to {{c1::sputum}}.
cards.question: Mucus, inflammatory cells and debris in inflamed airways contribute to {{c1::sputum}}.

cards.explanation: Surrounding vascular congestion accompanies the purulent lesion.
cards.text: The bacterial-pneumonia abscess contains neutrophils and {{c1::cellular debris}}.
cards.question: The bacterial-pneumonia abscess contains neutrophils and {{c1::cellular debris}}.

cards.explanation: It is favoured when the insult is removed, tissue destruction is limited and the affected cells can regenerate.
cards.text: Return to normal tissue after limited injury is {{c1::complete resolution}}.
cards.question: Return to normal tissue after limited injury is {{c1::complete resolution}}.

cards.explanation: Scar replaces lost tissue rather than perfectly restoring the original specialised cells.
cards.text: Substantial destruction of non-regenerating tissue favours healing by {{c1::fibrosis}}.
cards.question: Substantial destruction of non-regenerating tissue favours healing by {{c1::fibrosis}}.

cards.explanation: This is one outcome, not an inevitable stage for every acute response.
cards.text: Failure to eliminate a persistent stimulus can lead from acute to {{c1::chronic inflammation}}.
cards.question: Failure to eliminate a persistent stimulus can lead from acute to {{c1::chronic inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: The general repair model distinguishes these responses; they can occur together in different parts of a wound.
cards.text: Regeneration restores cells like those lost, whereas scar repair deposits {{c1::connective tissue}}.
cards.question: Regeneration restores cells like those lost, whereas scar repair deposits {{c1::connective tissue}}.

cards.explanation: Without termination signals, recruitment and vascular leakage may continue.
cards.text: Resolution requires removal or inactivation of inflammatory {{c1::chemical mediators}}.
cards.question: Resolution requires removal or inactivation of inflammatory {{c1::chemical mediators}}.

cards.explanation: Resolution also requires clearance of fluid already present, not merely closing the barrier.
cards.text: Normalisation of vascular permeability helps stop further {{c1::oedema formation}}.
cards.question: Normalisation of vascular permeability helps stop further {{c1::oedema formation}}.

cards.explanation: This is one component of clearance during resolution.
cards.text: Excess interstitial oedema fluid and proteins can leave through {{c1::lymphatic drainage}}.
cards.question: Excess interstitial oedema fluid and proteins can leave through {{c1::lymphatic drainage}}.

cards.explanation: Removal of dead cells and debris supports resolution rather than continued inflammatory injury.
cards.text: Macrophage clearance of apoptotic neutrophils helps terminate {{c1::acute inflammation}}.
cards.question: Macrophage clearance of apoptotic neutrophils helps terminate {{c1::acute inflammation}}.

cards.explanation: Their functions therefore connect inflammatory defence, resolution and healing.
cards.text: Besides clearing debris, macrophages release growth factors that promote {{c1::subsequent repair}}.
cards.question: Besides clearing debris, macrophages release growth factors that promote {{c1::subsequent repair}}.

Cytokines and Chemokines……..
Lets briefly clarify what they are before we move 
on….

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 4
slides.text:
Cytokines
•“Cytokines” are soluble protein mediators secreted by 
immune cells (mostly) that act on other cells to regulate 
their activity; many are called “interleukins” (IL-1, IL-2, 
etc.). 
•They are important in cell signalling (communication 
between cells).
•A subfamily of cytokines primarily functions in directing 
migration of cells, these are called “chemotactic 
cytokines” or “chemokines”

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 5
slides.text:
•
The major role of chemokines is to act as a chemoattractant to guide the 
migration of cells. (i.e. they attract leukocytes, recruiting monocytes, 
neutrophils from the blood to sites of infection or tissue damage). 
•
Some inflammatory chemokines activate cells to initiate an immune response 
or promote wound healing. They are released by many different cell types 
and serve to guide cells of both innate immune system and adaptive immune 
system.
•
Their release is often stimulated by pro-inflammatory cytokines such as 
interleukin 1.
Chemokines

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 6
slides.text:
Cytokines vs Chemokines
Cytokines and chemokines are proteins that regulate the processes of the 
immune system. They act as a messenger/postman trying to send signals/letters to 
cells in order to orhistrate/organise the ‘battle’ against infection. chemokines are a 
special type of cytokine that direct the migration of white blood cells to infected or 
damaged tissues.
“The difference between cytokines and chemokines lies in their function. 
A chemokine is a special type of cytokine whose main role is to guide the white 
blood cells to the affected area, a process which is known as chemotaxis. The white 
blood cells, along with lymphocytes, destroy any foreign microorganisms that may 
be causing the infection. They get rid of these pathogens to ensure that they don’t 
spread throughout the body. Once pathogens are removed, the healing process 
commences thanks to the cytokines”.
 (http://www.differencebetween.net/science/health/drugs-health/differences-between-cytokines-and-
chemokines/#ixzz3IIBxlxSN)

slides.text:
Inflammation 
Inflammare = to set on fire (Latin)
Inflammation is the body’s local physiological 
(protective) response to infection and tissue injury. 
It involves host cells, blood vessels and proteins.
It is the reaction of vascularized living tissue to local 
injury and it is induced by:
✓
Microbial infections
✓
Physical agents

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 15
slides.text:
Inflammatory response is normally self-limited 
and involves:
• Intravascular cells (white blood cells): Neutrophiles, 
monocytes, oesinophils, lymphocytes, basophils, platelets. Goal 
of inflammation is to bring those to the site of infection and/or 
tissue damage.
• Connective tissue cells: mast cells, fibroblasts, macrophages.
• Connective tissue matrix: structural proteins (collagen & 
elastin), glycoproteins (fibronectin & laminin), proteoglycan.
• Plasma proteins: fibrinogen, c-reactive protein etc.
• Chemical mediators produced by host cells: Cytokines (e.g. 
IL1), histamine, bradykinin, serotonin, protoglandins etc.

slides.text:
Main types of inflammation
Inflammation is usually classified according its time course 
and the cell types involved.
The two main types of inflammations are: 
Acute: 
•
which is the initial series of tissue responses to injury and 
may take a few hours to a few days. 
•
Its main characteristics are the exudation  of fluid and 
plasma proteins (oedema) and the emigration of leukocytes, 
predominantly neutrophils.
Chronic: 
•
Usually primary and prolonged responses but does 
occasionally follow the recurrent acute inflammation. 
•
It is associated histologically with the presence of 
lymphocytes and macrophages, the proliferation of blood 
vessels, fibrosis, and tissue injury.

Physical characteristics of acute inflammation
▪ Redness (rubor), e.g. skin sunburn 
▪ Heat (calor), due to vascular dilation and increased 
blood flow to the area
▪ Swelling (tumor), due to oedema (i.e. accumulation 
of fluid in extracellular space and the mass of 
inflammatory cells)
▪ Pain (dolor), due to stretching and distortion of 
tissues and from pus under pressure in an abscess 
cavity.  
▪ Loss of function, e.g. lack of movement

or frostbite; irradiation; some environmental chemicals)
• Tissue necrosis (from any cause) due to insufficient blood 
supply

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 40
slides.text:
❑Abscess is collection of pus (collection of dead neutrophils) in response to inflammation. 
❑Abscess formation is a defence mechanism to prevent infection from spreading to other 
parts of the body and arrest it locally.
❑Common sites of abscess formation are skin, lungs, teeth, tonsils, kidneys, brain, liver etc. 
How an abscess is formed?
▪
cytokines are released from the dead cells at the site of infection/injury.
▪
The released cytokines cause an inflammatory response, which increase blood flow and 
attract white blood cells (mainly neutrophils). 
▪
The while blood cells may die while fighting the infection. Due to presence of white blood 
cells, pus is usually white in colour. 
▪
The wall (or capsule) of the abscess is formed by adjoining healthy cells to prevent 
infection from spreading to neighbouring tissues. 
▪
However, presence of wall or capsule has disadvantage too. The abscess wall prevents 
the immune cells from attacking the bacteria in the pus and antibiotics from reaching the 
pus in abscess.
Abscess formation

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 46
slides.text:
Different stages of wound repair
Werner S. & Grose R. (2003) Physiol Rev 83: 
835
(A) 12-14h after injury: wound filled with blood 
clot. Neutrophils have invaded into the clot.
(B) 3-7 days after injury: most neutrophils have 
undergone apoptosis. Macrophages are 
abundant. Endothelial cells migrate into the 
clot; they proliferate and form new blood 
vessels, giving granular appearance - hence 
“granulation tissue”. Fibroblasts migrate into 
the wound tissue, proliferate and deposite 
ECM. Keratinocytes proliferate  and migrate 
in from the wound margins.
(C) 1-2 weeks after injury the wound is filled with 
granulation tissue. Fibroblasts have 
transformed into myofibroblasts leading to 
wound contraction, collagen deposition and 
scar formation.

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 47
slides.text:
Wound repair: Growth factors
•
Repair is initiated by the release of growth factors and cytokines from the 
serum of injured blood vessels and from degranulating platelets.
•
FGFs play a key role in wound healing. FGFs 1, 2, 7, 10 and 22 increased 
after injury.
•
Epithelial FGF receptors (FGFR1b and FGFR2b) known to bind FGFs 7, 
10 and 22 and shown to be important in wound reepithelialisation in 
knockout mouse studies.
•
Epidermal growth factor family (e.g.EGF, transforming growth factor- 
[TGF- ],heparin-binding EGF [HB-EGF]) are also important in 
reepithelialisation.
•
Other: VEGF (wound angiogenesis), HGF (angiogenesis, 
reepithelialisation and inflammation), IGFs and their receptors (pro-
proliferative and anti-apoptotic), chemokines (IL-10, IL-6, IL-8; multiple 
effects).

slides.text:
Complete resolution of acute 
inflammation
When:
1. The injury is limited or short-lived
2. The damaged parenchymal cells can regenerate
3. There has been little tissue destruction
How (mechanism):
1. Neutralization and removal of chemical mediators
2. Normalization of vascular permeability
3. Halting leukocyte emigration
4. Clearance of edema (Lymphatic drainage), inflammatory cells and 
necrotic debris (macrophages)

slides.topic: Inflammation I — Acute Inflammation & Repair — original page 60
slides.text:
Events in the resolution of 
inflammation
Modified from Henson PM: In Clark R, Henson PM (eds): The molecular and cell biology of wound repair. New York Plenum Press, 
1996). Robbins Basic pathology.
1. Return to normal vascular 
permeability
2. Drainage of edema fluid and proteins 
into lymphatics
3. pinocytosis into macrophages
4. phagocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils
5. phagocytosis of necrotic debris
6. disposal of macrophages
Macrophages also produce growth 
factors that initiate the subsequent 
process of repair
